name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,165

clue.text: Nuts in biscuits

blocks.note: first meaning: mad, out of one's mind
second meaning: thin dry savoury biscuits, often eaten with cheese

explanation.surface: Someone describes biscuits with nuts baked into them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' reads as an ingredient, but it is an adjective meaning crazy; 'in' merely joins the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: informal slang for insane, and the plural noun for plain savoury wafers eaten with cheese.

clue.text: Get in touch with every individual after run

indicators.note: one thing coming after another tells us which piece is written second in the line

blocks.note: R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a run
every individual one, taken one at a time

explanation.surface: Advice to contact everyone personally once a run is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The run letter is placed first because the other piece comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To contact someone, for instance by phone, is a common modern sense of the verb, as in 'I couldn't manage to contact her'.

clue.text: Discipline cat misbehaving with hens

indicators.note: something misbehaving will not stay in its proper order, so its letters get rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cat that chases the hens needs to be disciplined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discipline' looks like an order about the cat, but it is the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To chasten is to correct or restrain someone by punishment, a close synonym of the verb sense.

clue.text: Jacob perhaps initially educated with Esau

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so we keep only the opening letter of each following word

blocks.note: the first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A Bible scene: Jacob schooled alongside his twin brother Esau.
explanation.walkthrough: The Biblical names lure you to Genesis, but Jacob is also a breed of piebald sheep; 'perhaps' warns that it is only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A Jacob is a breed of domestic sheep, so a female of that breed is an example of a female sheep.

clue.text: Place above great facade

blocks.note: super is informal for great or excellent
a pose is a false front put on for show

explanation.surface: A building with a grand frontage placed over it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place' reads as a noun for a location, but here it is a verb, and 'Place above' together is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To superpose is to lay one thing over or on top of another, a technical verb used in geometry and physics.

clue.text: Rock band’s source of inspiration

blocks.note: first meaning: the English rock group from Devon, famous for 'Supermassive Black Hole'
second meaning: a person or goddess who inspires an artist

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s looks possessive, as if asking where the group gets its ideas, but it stands for 'is', linking two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The nine Greek goddesses who inspired the arts gave their name to any person who inspires creative work, and a British rock trio took that name.

clue.text: Planet with hot wet region

blocks.note: the red planet, fourth from the sun
H is the standard abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A description of a planet with a steamy, swampy zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot' seems to describe the region, but it supplies a single letter tacked onto the planet.
explanation.definitionFit: A marsh is low land that is waterlogged much of the time, so it is fairly called a soggy area of ground.

clue.text: Manifest or agenda contains space to put items

indicators.note: a phrase that contains something holds it inside its own run of letters

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A shipping manifest or a meeting agenda lists where cargo or business will go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manifest' tempts as a verb or adjective, but it is just a container of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Storage is room set aside for keeping goods and belongings, as in a storage cupboard or unit.

clue.text: Set down outside a royal residence

indicators.note: one thing placed outside another wraps around it on both sides

blocks.note: to place something is to set it down
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something is put down outside the gates of a royal home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set down outside' sounds like a location, but 'outside' tells you the verb's letters wrap round the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A palace is the official home of a monarch, so the phrase is a straightforward descriptive synonym.

clue.text: Bird arrives in vessel

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a pot is a vessel for cooking or holding things
ARR is the abbreviation for arrives on a timetable

explanation.surface: A bird lands aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a boat, but here it is a cooking pot; ARR is the abbreviation seen on arrivals boards.
explanation.definitionFit: A parrot is a type of tropical bird with a hooked beak, so the general term covers it as an example.

clue.text: Ruined tree removed from army town

indicators.note: something removed from a word is taken out, leaving the rest behind

blocks.note: Aldershot is a Hampshire town known as the home of the British Army
the alder is a tree of damp ground

explanation.surface: A garrison town whose ruined tree has been cleared away.
explanation.walkthrough: Aldershot, in southern England, is the traditional home of the British Army; lose the alder and four letters remain.
explanation.definitionFit: Shot is informal for worn out or wrecked, as in 'my nerves are shot', matching the adjective sense.

clue.text: Dry habit abandoned for celebration

indicators.note: abandoned also means wild and unrestrained, so these letters run loose into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A teetotaller gives up abstaining for a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandoned' looks like 'given up' in the surface story, but it works in its sense of wild and uncontrolled.
explanation.definitionFit: A birthday is the annual party or occasion marking the day someone was born, a specific example of a festivity.

clue.text: Game bird is all excited

indicators.note: something excited is stirred up and agitated, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A game bird such as a pheasant gets all worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game bird' looks like a single phrase; it splits, with 'Game' as the definition and 'bird' starting the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Billiards is a cue sport played on a cloth-covered table with balls, so it is an example of a game.

clue.text: What may be used for shipping tin and aluminium

definitions.text: What may be used for shipping

blocks.note: a tin is a can
Al is the chemical symbol for aluminium

explanation.surface: Tin and aluminium are metals that might be shipped as freight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tin' and 'aluminium' look like a cargo of metals, but one is a container and the other a chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Canals are artificial waterways built to carry barges and boats of goods, so they are a means of transporting freight.

clue.text: Bottle about as old as we are?

blocks.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
someone as old as us is of our own years

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a bottle, perhaps of wine, dates from the same year we were born.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' seems a container, but in British slang it means nerve or daring, as in 'he lost his bottle'.
explanation.definitionFit: In British informal speech bottle means nerve or bravery, so the slang term and the standard noun are synonyms.

clue.text: Odd and blooming concerning

blocks.note: flowers that are blooming are out
re means about or concerning, as in letter headings

explanation.surface: A comment on something both strange and flowering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' could be a mild British expletive, but here it means in flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Outré, borrowed from French, describes something unconventional or bizarre, close in sense to strange or peculiar.

clue.text: Small canine, one attempting to get round Queen Elizabeth

indicators.note: getting round something means surrounding it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: a trier is someone who tries or attempts
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A little dog trying to circle round the late monarch, famous for her corgis.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the royal cipher of Queen Elizabeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Terriers are a group of mostly compact, lively dog breeds originally bred for hunting vermin, an example of a little dog.

clue.text: Mongrel with a vet I arranged making things better

indicators.note: arranged means put into a chosen order, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: a cur is a mongrel dog
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mixed-breed dog and a vet booking an appointment to help it recover.
explanation.walkthrough: The vet suggests healing in the surface, but only the letters of 'a vet I' are rearranged after the dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Something curative restores health or remedies a problem, so it serves to improve or heal.

clue.text: A new hair preparation? A heavenly one

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
gel is a styling product for hair

explanation.surface: An advert asks whether a new hair product is divine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A heavenly one' sounds like praise for the product, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An angel is a spiritual being from paradise in religious belief, so a heavenly creature describes one.

clue.text: Stack building blocks without covers

indicators.note: covers are the outside layers, and going without them strips off both ends

blocks.note: bricks are the blocks used in building

explanation.surface: An instruction to pile up toy blocks without their boxes.
explanation.walkthrough: A rick is a large stack of hay or straw, as in hayrick.
explanation.definitionFit: A rick is a stack of hay, corn or straw built in a field, so the noun sense is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Rare item — collectors usually rate it outstanding at the outset

indicators.note: the outset is the beginning, so only each word's opening letter counts

blocks.note: the first letters of the five words

explanation.surface: Collectors tend to judge a rare find exceptional right from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a fair statement about collectors, which is why the first-letter trick is easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: A curio is an unusual or interesting object valued as a collectible, so it is a rarity or uncommon piece.

clue.text: Risk the heart of Andes range collapsing

indicators.note: a heart is the centre, so only the middle letter is kept
a thing collapsing falls apart and its parts land in a new order

blocks.note: the central letter of the five-letter mountain name
taken as written

explanation.surface: Mountaineers fear the central Andes falling in on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Andes range' reads as one place, but 'range' is fodder to rearrange, not part of the mountains' name.
explanation.definitionFit: Danger and risk both name the chance of harm or loss, so the nouns are close synonyms.

clue.text: Railway by a Roman road where rails might be seen?

blocks.note: taken as written
via is Latin for road, as in the Via Appia
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A railway line running beside an old Roman road, where track would be visible.
explanation.walkthrough: The rails seem to be railway lines, but a rail is also a wading marsh bird; 'by' places the railway after the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Rails are a family of birds, and an aviary is an enclosure for keeping birds, so you might find them there.

clue.text: Silver ring in the past

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a ring is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: A silver wedding ring from years gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver ring' reads as jewellery, but splits into a chemical symbol and a round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ago means before now, back in time, so it is an adverb equal to the phrase about earlier times.

clue.text: We are going to fit spring successfully

blocks.note: a contraction of 'we will', written without its apostrophe
healthy, in good shape
a source of water from the ground
in a satisfactory manner

explanation.walkthrough: The clue strings together four separate meanings of one short word; reading 'spring' as a season or 'fit' as a seizure leads astray.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works as an adjective for being in good health and as a noun for a source of water drawn from underground.

clue.text: Location to display car’s performance and capacity?

blocks.note: a show is a performance on stage
room is space or capacity, as in room for six

explanation.surface: A motoring review of a car's speed and boot space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Performance and capacity' sound like car specifications, but each word yields a piece; the apostrophe-s turns the definition into 'car is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A showroom is a sales area where dealers put vehicles or goods on view for customers to inspect.
